rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which property of transition metals enables them to form alloys ?
rows.solution:
An alloy forms when atoms of one metal replace atoms of another in the same crystal lattice, and that substitution only works if the two kinds of atom are nearly the same size. Transition metals of a given series have very SIMILAR ATOMIC RADII, because each added electron goes into an inner d orbital and screens the growing nuclear charge fairly well, so the radius changes little across the series. They therefore substitute for one another readily and form alloys freely — steel, brass and bronze among them.

High ionisation enthalpy, catalytic activity and complex formation are all genuine properties of transition metals, but none of them has anything to do with fitting into another metal's lattice.

rows.stem: Which of the following d-orbitals experience more repulsion in the crystal field splitting of tetrahedral complex ?
rows.solution:
A tetrahedral field is the inverse of an octahedral one. The four ligands do NOT approach along the axes; they sit at alternate corners of a cube, so they come closer to the regions BETWEEN the axes. The orbitals whose lobes point between the axes — \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{yz}\) and \(d_{xz}\), the \(t_2\) set — therefore meet the ligands more directly and are repelled more, so they are raised in energy. The \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{z^2}\) orbitals, whose lobes lie along the axes, are further from the ligands and are lowered; they form the \(e\) set.

So the splitting is upside down compared with the octahedral case, and it is also smaller — \(\Delta_t\) is about four-ninths of \(\Delta_0\) for the same ligands, which is why low spin tetrahedral complexes are so rare.

rows.stem: The position of – Br in the compound \(\mathrm{C_6H_5 - CH = CH - CH(Br) - CH_3}\) can be classified as :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE – the compound is printed with its benzene ring as a SKELETAL DRAWING carrying the typed chain – CH = CH – CH(Br) – CH3 (the Br hangs below the third chain carbon on a vertical bond; confirmed at 3x). It is NAMED losslessly in the stem as C6H5 – CH = CH – CH(Br) – CH3, so the row is answerable from text: the reader must still classify the position, which no option letter is stated by. Page idx 2.
rows.solution:
Classify a halide by what the carbon carrying the halogen is attached to. Here that carbon is attached to \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\), to \(-\mathrm{H}\), and to the carbon of a \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond — it is the carbon NEXT TO the double bond, not part of it. A halogen on the carbon adjacent to a double bond is ALLYLIC.

A vinylic halide would have the halogen on a doubly bonded carbon itself, an aryl halide on a ring carbon, and a benzylic halide on the carbon directly attached to a benzene ring. Here the ring is two carbons away, so benzylic does not apply either.

rows.stem: Williamson synthesis is an example of :
rows.solution:
Williamson synthesis prepares an ether by treating an alkyl halide with a sodium alkoxide:
\(\mathrm{R-ONa} + \mathrm{R'-X} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-O-R'} + \mathrm{NaX}\)

The alkoxide ion is a nucleophile; it attacks the carbon bearing the halogen and displaces the halide. That is a nucleophilic SUBSTITUTION, specifically an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction — which is why the method works best with primary halides and fails with tertiary ones, where elimination takes over instead.

rows.stem: Number of possible stereoisomers for the complex \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]Cl}\) will be :
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\) is octahedral with two bidentate ligands and two chlorides, so the two chlorides may be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans). That gives two geometrical isomers — but the count does not stop there.

The TRANS isomer has a plane of symmetry and so is optically inactive: one form. The CIS isomer has no plane of symmetry, so it is chiral and exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images: two forms.

The total number of stereoisomers is therefore \(1 + 2 = 3\).

rows.stem: The correct order of decreasing basic strength of \(\mathrm{CH_3 - NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\) and \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\) in aqueous solution is :
rows.solution:
For METHYL groups the three competing effects settle differently from ethyl ones, and that is what this question tests. The inductive effect favours the tertiary amine; steric crowding and, more importantly, solvation favour the primary one, since \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_3^+}\) has three hydrogens on nitrogen to hydrogen bond with water while \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{NH^+}\) has only one.

With the small methyl group the balance puts the secondary amine first, the primary second and the tertiary last:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH} > \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} > (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N}\)
Note the order is NOT the same as for ethyl groups, where the tertiary amine moves ahead of the primary — the bulkier the alkyl group, the more the balance shifts.

rows.stem: Which of the following reagent is used to convert benzene diazonium chloride to benzene ?
rows.solution:
Ethanol reduces the diazonium group, supplying a hydrogen atom in its place while nitrogen leaves as gas; the ethanol is oxidised to ethanal:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_6} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
Hypophosphorous acid with water does the same job and is the other standard reagent.

Water would give phenol rather than benzene, and cuprous cyanide would give benzonitrile — both replacements, but by a group rather than by hydrogen.

rows.stem: Which of the following is a water-soluble vitamin ?
rows.solution:
The B group vitamins are water soluble, as is vitamin C. Being water soluble, they are not stored in the body: any excess is excreted in the urine, so they must be supplied in the diet regularly.

Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat soluble. They are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue, which is why an excess of THOSE can accumulate and become harmful.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Alcohols act as Bronsted bases as well as Bronsted acids.
Reason (R) : Alcohols react as both nucleophiles and electrophiles.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Alcohols do act as both Bronsted acids and Bronsted bases, so the Assertion is true: the polar \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond lets them donate a proton, as in their reaction with sodium, and the lone pairs on oxygen let them accept one, as in the first step of acid catalysed dehydration. Alcohols also act as both nucleophiles and electrophiles, so the Reason is true as well.

But the two statements concern different classifications. Bronsted acid and base are about PROTON transfer; nucleophile and electrophile are about ELECTRON-PAIR donation and acceptance to carbon. Both behaviours trace back to the same oxygen, but neither statement explains the other. So both are true and the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are more stable than those of aliphatic amines.
Reason (R) : Diazonium salts of aromatic amines undergo resonance.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Aromatic diazonium salts are far more stable than aliphatic ones — stable enough to be isolated at low temperature, where the aliphatic ones decompose at once — so the Assertion is true. And the Reason names the cause correctly: in an aryl diazonium ion the positive charge is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, which spreads it out and stabilises the ion. An aliphatic diazonium ion has no such delocalisation and loses nitrogen immediately to give a carbocation. The Reason is therefore the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : For complex reaction, order of reaction is given by the fast step.
Reason (R) : Order of reaction is determined experimentally.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
For a complex reaction the order is set by the SLOWEST step, the rate-determining step, not by the fast one — a fast step that follows the slow one cannot influence the overall rate. So the Assertion is false.

The Reason is true: order is determined experimentally, from the measured rate law, rather than read off the balanced equation. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Cu^{2+}/Cu}}\) has positive value (+ \(0{\cdot}34\) V).
Reason (R) : It is due to low \(\mathrm{\Delta_{hyd}H^{o}}\) and high \(\mathrm{\Delta_{a}H^{o}}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The standard electrode potential of the copper couple is indeed positive, \(+0.34\) V, uniquely so in the first transition series, so the Assertion is true. And the Reason gives the cause: forming \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) from the metal in water requires atomising the metal and then ionising it twice, and copper's enthalpy of atomisation is high while the hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is not large enough to repay those costs. The overall energy balance is unfavourable, which is what a positive \(E^{\circ}\) records — copper is not oxidised by \(\mathrm{H^+}\), which is why it does not liberate hydrogen from dilute acids. The Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Write the formulas for the following coordination compounds :
(a) Mercury(I) tetrathiocyanato-S-cobaltate(III)
(b) Dichloridobis (ethane-1,2-diamine) platinum(IV) nitrate
rows.solution:
(a) Mercury(I) tetrathiocyanato-S-cobaltate(III). The anion contains cobalt at \(+3\) with four thiocyanato ligands, each \(-1\), so the complex ion carries \(3 - 4 = -1\) and needs one mercury(I) ion to balance it. The \(-S\) in the name says the thiocyanate is bound through its sulphur atom rather than its nitrogen.
\(\mathrm{Hg[Co(SCN)_4]}\)

(b) Dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)platinum(IV) nitrate. Inside the sphere are two chlorido ligands at \(-1\) each and two neutral ethane-1,2-diamine ligands, with platinum at \(+4\), so the complex cation is \(4 - 2 = +2\) and two nitrate ions are needed outside.
\(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2Cl_2](NO_3)_2}\)

rows.stem: Name the sugar present in sugarcane. What are the hydrolysis products of this sugar ? Is this sugar a reducing sugar ?
rows.solution:
The sugar present in sugarcane is sucrose.

On hydrolysis it gives one molecule of D-(+)-glucose and one of D-(−)-fructose:
\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} + \mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

No, sucrose is NOT a reducing sugar. Its glycosidic linkage joins C-1 of the glucose unit to C-2 of the fructose unit — that is, it ties up the reducing group of BOTH units — so neither a free aldehydic nor a free ketonic group remains to reduce Tollens' reagent or Fehling's solution. Maltose and lactose, whose linkages leave one reducing group free, are reducing sugars.

rows.stem:
Draw the structures of major products in each of the following reactions :
(a) Chlorobenzene \(\mathrm{+\ CH_3 - Cl}\) \(\xrightarrow[\text{Dry Ether}]{\mathrm{Na}}\)
(b) 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)phenol \(\mathrm{+\ HBr \longrightarrow}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE – both substrates are printed as SKELETAL DRAWINGS: (a) a benzene ring carrying Cl, and (b) a benzene ring carrying HO and CH2CH2OH at PARA positions (1,4 confirmed at 3x by counting ring vertices). Both are NAMED losslessly in the stem (chlorobenzene; 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)phenol, equivalently 2-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethanol), so the row is answerable from text, and the question asks for the PRODUCTS, so naming a reactant cannot state the answer. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) This is the Wurtz-Fittig reaction: sodium in dry ether couples the aryl halide to the alkyl halide through the two carbons that carried the halogens.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Cl} + \mathrm{CH_3Cl} + 2\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)
The major product is toluene.

(b) The molecule has two hydroxyl groups and only ONE of them reacts, which is the whole point. The alcoholic \(-\mathrm{OH}\) on the side chain is replaced by bromine in the ordinary way. The PHENOLIC \(-\mathrm{OH}\) is not touched: its oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond has partial double bond character and is too strong for hydrogen bromide to break.
\(\mathrm{HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2CH_2OH} + \mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2CH_2Br} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
The major product is 4-(2-bromoethyl)phenol.

rows.stem:
Give the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions :
(a) Aniline \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{Br_2}}\) A \(\xrightarrow[0 - 5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}}\) B \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3PO_2 + H_2O}}\) C
(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3 - Cl}\) \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{KCN}}\) A \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}}\) B \(\xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{CHCl_3 + alc.\ KOH}}\) C
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE – part (a)'s substrate is printed as a SKELETAL DRAWING of a benzene ring carrying NH2. It is NAMED losslessly in the stem as Aniline, so the row is answerable from text; the question asks for A, B and C, so naming the reactant cannot state the answer. Part (b) is fully typed and carries no drawing. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) Bromine water brominates aniline at all three activated positions at once, since the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group is too strongly activating for the reaction to stop at one:
\(\mathrm{A} = \) 2,4,6-tribromoaniline
Sodium nitrite in hydrochloric acid at \(0-5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) diazotises the remaining amino group:
\(\mathrm{B} = \) 2,4,6-tribromobenzenediazonium chloride
Hypophosphorous acid with water then replaces the diazonium group by hydrogen:
\(\mathrm{C} = \) 1,3,5-tribromobenzene
The sequence is the standard way of reaching a 1,3,5-trisubstituted ring, which direct bromination of benzene could never give — the amino group directs the three bromines into place and is then removed.

(b) Potassium cyanide is ionic, so the free cyanide ion attacks through its CARBON and gives the alkyl cyanide:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CN}\), ethanenitrile
Lithium aluminium hydride reduces the nitrile all the way to the primary amine, keeping both carbons:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\), ethylamine
Chloroform with alcoholic potassium hydroxide is the carbylamine reaction, which converts a primary amine to the isocyanide:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2NC}\), ethyl isocyanide
Note the route has gone from cyanide to ISOcyanide: the carbon-attached nitrile became an amine, and the nitrogen then attacked to give the nitrogen-attached isomer.
